renderSubtitles.text:
A gene comes in two forms. Big A has frequency p.
Little a has frequency q.

Between them they make up everything:
p plus q is one.

Every child gets one allele from each parent,
at random.

So draw a square. Along the top, one parent's alleles.
Down the side, the other's.

Cut where each side splits
into p and q.

Each piece is one kind of child, and its area
is how common that kind is.

Both parents give A: p times p.
That is p squared.

One gives A and the other gives a. There are two ways,
so two rectangles: two p q.

Both give little a: q times q.
That is q squared.

Now count the alleles in all these children.
Each child carries two.

Send every A to one bin,
and every little a to the other.

Out of fifty alleles, thirty are A,
and twenty are little a.

Measure the bins with the same two rulers that
measured the parents: p, and q. They match.

The allele frequencies have not changed.
Random mating only shuffles them into new pairs.

That holds when mating is random, with no selection,
no mutation, no migration, and a large population.

Put the pieces back together: the whole square,
the whole population. Area one.

So p squared, plus two p q, plus q squared,
equals one.

That is the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium: p and q stay fixed,
so these proportions return, generation after generation.
